title: Sea Anemones Flip the Script on Antiviral Defense
summary: For decades, scientists believed that animals inherited a core antiviral defense system from a common ancestor. But a new study on sea anemones is turning that assumption on its head. Researchers at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem, led by PhD candidate Ton Sharoni and Professor Yehu Moran, have discovered a protein that looks like one of our most important virus-fighters but does the exact opposite—and it's essential for survival. In humans, the protein MAVS acts as a critical alarm. When a virus is detected, MAVS triggers a cascade of immune responses. The team expected to find a similar system in sea anemones, which branched off from our evolutionary line over 600 million years ago. Instead, they found CARDIB (CARD Inhibitor Binding protein). At first glance, CARDIB seemed like a MAVS twin. "Everything about CARDIB suggested it should function like MAVS," said Moran. "Instead, we discovered that it does the exact opposite. Rather than activating antiviral defenses, CARDIB normally suppresses them." This raised a puzzling question: why would an animal deliberately dampen its own immune response? To find out, the team used CRISPR gene editing to knock out the CARDIB gene in sea anemones and then exposed them to viruses. The results were counterintuitive. Anemones without CARDIB became far more susceptible to infection. Viruses replicated rapidly, and the animals failed to mount an effective antiviral response. "Although CARDIB acts as a brake on the immune system under normal conditions, that brake turns out to be essential for mounting an effective antiviral response," explained Sharoni. The researchers then moved genetically modified anemones from lab tanks to outdoor marine mesocosms in South Carolina, exposing them to a natural cocktail of viruses. Within days, anemones lacking CARDIB accumulated significantly more viruses. One immune gene that seemed only moderately important in the lab proved crucial in the wild. "This demonstrated that the pathway we discovered is not simply a laboratory phenomenon," said Moran. "It plays a crucial role in helping these animals cope with the viral challenges they face in nature." The findings, published in Nature Ecology & Evolution, suggest that evolution did not settle on a single antiviral strategy. Different animal groups may have independently developed distinct molecular systems for detecting and fighting viruses. This discovery opens new avenues for understanding immune diversity and could eventually inspire novel antiviral therapies.
why_it_matters: This discovery rewrites what we know about how immune systems evolved. For a teenager today, it means that nature has more than one blueprint for fighting viruses—insights that could someday inspire totally new classes of medicines, especially as viruses continue to pose global challenges.

background_read: Sea anemones, which look like colorful flowers on the ocean floor, branched off from the evolutionary line leading to humans over 600 million years ago. They are part of the phylum Cnidaria, which also includes jellyfish and corals. Because they diverged so early, studying their immune systems can reveal what ancient animal defenses might have looked like.

In humans and other vertebrates, a key virus alarm is the protein MAVS (Mitochondrial Antiviral-Signaling protein). When MAVS senses a virus, it triggers a cascade of immune signals. Scientists at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem (a major research university in Israel) wanted to trace this defensive pathway back in time by looking at invertebrates like the sea anemone.

The research team, led by PhD candidate Ton Sharoni and Professor Yehu Moran, used CRISPR (a powerful gene-editing technology that can precisely cut and disable specific genes) to create anemones missing the newly discovered protein CARDIB. They then exposed the animals to viruses in both sterile lab tanks and outdoor marine mesocosms in South Carolina—large tanks that mimic real ocean conditions—to see how the loss affected survival. The striking results, reported in the journal Nature Ecology & Evolution (a top venue for evolutionary research), challenge the long-held belief that all animals share the same fundamental antiviral strategy.

perspectives.description: The finding that a brake on the immune system is actually crucial for fighting viruses is a major conceptual leap. It opens a whole new area of research into how different animals defend themselves, which could lead to therapies that tweak immune responses in humans without causing harmful overreactions.

While promising, the work was done in a very simple animal. There is a long road from a sea anemone protein to a human drug, and the dual role of CARDIB—both protecting and potentially weakening the organism—means that manipulating similar systems in people could have unexpected and dangerous side effects.

Evolution is opportunistic: it can repurpose ancient molecular parts for new jobs. The fact that a MAVS-like structure became a suppressor in anemones illustrates how immune systems are not a single, conserved machine but a collection of independently assembled solutions. This challenges the idea that all complex life shares one core antiviral pathway.

Next, scientists will likely look for CARDIB-like proteins in other invertebrates and even in early vertebrates. Understanding how the 'brake and accelerator' of immunity are balanced could help design drugs that fine-tune our own immune systems—either to boost them against infections or to calm them down in autoimmune diseases.
